title: Interest and compounding
summary: Money today is worth more than the same money later. Simple interest pays on the principal only; compound interest pays on interest too, and how often it compounds changes the real rate.
objectives: Explain why money has a time value.
Work out simple and compound interest with a formula.
Compound more than once a year, and convert a nominal rate to an effective rate with EFFECT.
Estimate doubling time with the rule of 72.

p: ₹1 lakh today is worth more than ₹1 lakh next year, because today’s lakh can earn interest in the meantime.
Every finance decision compares money at different times: a loan, a deposit, an investment.
To compare, move all the money to **one date** using an interest rate.
That idea, the **time value of money**, sits under every lesson in this course.
In real life: got a ₹1 lakh Diwali bonus. A relative offered to keep it safe and hand back ₹1 lakh in five years. A 7% deposit would hand back ₹1,40,255.

slides.h: Simple interest: on the principal only
p: Simple interest pays the same amount every year: principal × rate × years. Interest never earns interest.
Each year earns the same ₹7,000.
Flat-rate loans charge interest this way, which makes them dearer than they look (Lesson 2.4).
In real life: quotes gold loans at “1.5% a month”. The interest is worked out on the full loan every month, simple interest, so a ₹50,000 loan costs ₹750 a month however much has been repaid.

p: With compounding, each year’s interest joins the balance and earns interest too. The gap with simple interest starts small, then runs away.
In Excel: `=B2*(1+B3)^B4`. The **^** raises (1 + rate) to the power of the years.
After 5 years the gap is small: ₹1,40,255 against ₹1,35,000.
After 30 years compounding gives more than twice as much.
In real life: put ₹10,000 in a cumulative deposit when Meera was born and renewed it every time it matured. At about 7% it is now worth about ₹66,488.

check.q: ₹1,00,000 at 7% compounded yearly for 2 years. What is it worth?
check.explain: ₹1,00,000 × 1.07 × 1.07 = ₹1,14,490. The second year earns interest on ₹1,07,000, not just on ₹1,00,000.

why.0: That’s simple interest: it ignores the interest earned on the first year’s interest.
why.3: That multiplies by 1.49; the rate is 7% a year.

p: Many deposits add interest quarterly or monthly. Divide the rate by the times a year, and multiply the years by it.
Quarterly: `=B2*(1+B3/4)^(B4*4)`: 1.75% a quarter, 20 quarters.
More often earns a little more, but the gain shrinks: daily is barely ahead of monthly.
Many Indian bank deposits compound quarterly. The deposit’s terms say which.
In real life: compared two 7% deposits. One compounds yearly, the other quarterly. On ₹1 lakh over 5 years the quarterly one pays ₹1,223 more, for nothing.

p: A deposit at “7% compounded quarterly” really earns 7.19% a year. The 7% is the **nominal** rate; 7.19% is the **effective** rate.
`=EFFECT(nominal rate, times a year)` gives the effective rate.
`=NOMINAL(effective rate, times a year)` goes back the other way.
Compare offers on **effective** rates, never on the headline numbers.
In real life: advertised 7.25% compounded yearly and 7.05% compounded monthly. The second sounds worse, but its effective rate is 7.28%: the better deal.

p: To guess how long money takes to double, divide 72 by the yearly rate in %. It’s close enough to check any offer in your head.
Accurate for rates from about 4% to 15%.
It works backwards too: to double in 6 years you need about 12% a year.
Lesson 1.4’s PDURATION gives the exact answer.
In real life: checks every investment pitch with it. A scheme promising to “double your money in 3 years” needs 24% a year. That’s a warning sign, not an offer.

check.q: Deposit A pays 7.20% compounded yearly. Deposit B pays 7.00% compounded monthly. Which earns more?
options: You can’t tell without the amount
check.explain: =EFFECT(7%,12) is 7.23%, a little more than A’s 7.20%. Monthly compounding beats the higher headline rate.

why.0: Headline rates hide the compounding. Compare effective rates.
why.3: The amount doesn’t change which rate is higher.

demo.intro: Work out Meera’s deposit in Excel: compound it yearly, then quarterly, then find the effective rate.

frames.say: In **B9** type `=B2*(1+B3)^B4`: the deposit times (1 + rate), raised to the power of the years. Meera’s ₹1 lakh grows to ₹1,40,255.
Quarterly compounding: divide the rate by **B5** (4) and multiply the years by it: `=B2*(1+B3/B5)^(B4*B5)`. ₹1,41,478.
**Formulas › Financial › EFFECT** opens Function Arguments. Nominal_rate **B3**, Npery **B5**: the effective rate is 7.19%.
Every answer points at the inputs. Change the rate in B3 and the whole sheet updates.

lab.intro: Meera has ₹1,00,000 to put in a 5-year deposit at 7%. The inputs are in **B2:B5**, and three banks’ offers are in **D2:F5**. Work out each answer with a formula that points at the inputs.

tasks.prompt: In **B8**, work out the **simple interest** Meera would earn over the five years.
hints: Simple interest = principal × rate × years.
The deposit is B2, the rate B3, the years B4.

tasks.prompt: In **B9**, work out what the deposit is worth after five years, **compounded yearly**.
hints: Multiply by (1 + rate) once for each year.
Use ^ for “to the power of”.

mistakes.msg: That multiplies by the years, which is simple interest. Raise (1 + rate) to the power of the years: (1+B3)^B4.
Put brackets round 1+B3 before raising it to the power: (1+B3)^B4.

tasks.prompt: In **B10**, work out the value after five years if interest is **compounded quarterly** (B5 times a year).
hints: Divide the yearly rate by the times a year.
Multiply the years by the times a year.

mistakes.msg: Divide the rate by the times a year: (1+B3/B5).
Raise it to the number of quarters: the years times B5, in brackets: ^(B4*B5).

tasks.prompt: In **B11**, find the deposit’s **effective annual rate** with EFFECT.
hints: EFFECT takes the nominal rate and the times a year.
=EFFECT(nominal_rate, npery)
=EFFECT(B3,B5)

tasks.prompt: In **G3:G5**, work out each bank’s **effective rate**. Write it in G3 and fill down.
hints: Each bank’s nominal rate is in column E, the times a year in column F.
=EFFECT(E3,F3), then fill down to G5.
=EFFECT(E3,F3)

tasks.prompt: Which bank pays Meera the most?
hints: Compare column G, not column E.
The differences are in the third decimal.
Quarterly compounding at 7% just beats monthly at 6.95%.
tasks.explain: Bank C’s 7% compounded quarterly is worth 7.186% a year, just ahead of Bank B and well ahead of Bank A’s 7.10% compounded yearly.
options: Bank A: it has the highest headline rate

why.0: Bank A compounds once a year, so 7.10% is all it pays.
why.1: Close, but 7.176% is just below Bank C’s 7.186%.

tasks.prompt: In **B12**, estimate how many years Meera’s money takes to **double**, with the rule of 72.
hints: Divide 72 by the rate written as a whole number.
B3 holds 0.07, so multiply it by 100 first.

mistakes.msg: B3 holds 0.07, so 72/B3 gives 1,028. Multiply B3 by 100 first: =72/(B3*100).

quiz.q: Why is ₹1 lakh today worth more than ₹1 lakh in a year?
options: Today’s money can earn interest in the meantime
It isn’t; they’re worth the same
quiz.explain: That’s the time value of money: money now can be invested and grow.

quiz.q: ₹50,000 at 8% simple interest for 3 years earns how much interest?

why.3: That’s the final balance, not the interest.

quiz.q: What does `=B2*(1+B3)^B4` give when B2 is 1,00,000, B3 is 10% and B4 is 2?
A deposit pays 8% compounded quarterly. Which formula gives its value after 3 years on ₹1 lakh in B2?

quiz.explain: 1% a month compounded for 12 months is 12.68% a year.

quiz.q: By the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 9% a year?

points: Money now is worth more than money later, because it can **earn interest**.
**Simple** interest: principal × rate × years. **Compound**: `=P*(1+r)^n`, and for k times a year `=P*(1+r/k)^(n*k)`.
Compare offers on the **effective** rate (`=EFFECT(rate, k)`); the **rule of 72** gives doubling time.
recap.cheat: Compound value = P×(1+r)^n; compare offers with =EFFECT(rate, times a year).

cards.back: **Simple**: interest on the principal only. **Compound**: interest on interest too.

cards.front: Value of P after n years at r, compounded yearly

cards.back: Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ the rate in %. At 8%: about 9 years.

cards.front: In **B4**, the value of B1 after B3 years at B2, compounded yearly.
